hints.title: Keep the sign of the multiplier
hints.body: Multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction; a positive multiplier preserves it. A multiplier not given a sign needs separate consideration.
hints.recap: An algebraic operation is valid only with the required sign condition.
hints.pitfall: Equality cases alone cannot settle a statement about all allowed values.
hints.pause: Apply this rule to the first and third proposed inequalities, including negative choices for an unrestricted multiplier.

recall.reminder: Check sign assumptions before transforming an inequality.

hints.title: Look for a square in the second statement
hints.body: Move the terms of the second inequality to one side. Compare the result with the expansion of a squared difference.
hints.recap: A square of a real quantity is nonnegative.
hints.pitfall: For a universal claim, a few successful examples are weaker than an identity.
hints.pause: Factor the difference, then assemble your conclusions for all three statements.

recall.reminder: Use a general identity to prove a claim or an allowed example to disprove it.

solution:
Statement 1 is true because a≥b gives −b≥−a. Statement 2 is true because a2+b2−2ab=(a−b)2≥0.

Statement 3 fails at a=2,b=1,c=−1: it would require −2≥−1. Thus only 1 and 2 are always true. Answer E.
